ref: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 67.2
basis: many dwellings in the Father's house
note: Augustine reads John 14's many dwellings as the differing places of blessedness in God's one house, making the destination more than a passing lodging.
The Didache directs the community to gather, give thanks, and make its sacrifice pure; it is an early Christian liturgical continuation of gathered worship and offering.
Justin identifies Malachi's pure offering with Christian Eucharistic bread and cup, changing the prophetic name-and-offering text into a communal Christian rite.

basis: Christ interpreted as the Passover lamb
note: The commentary describes an animal brought for sacrifice; Paul identifies Christ as the Passover lamb sacrificed and uses that reading to frame the community's feast.
Paul calls Christ the sacrificed Passover; read beside Exodus 12, it recasts the household-protecting sacrificial pattern through Christ rather than a Temple-bound animal.

basis: the community as a spiritual house
note: The commentary describes livestock brought to a House for worship; Peter calls believers living stones in a spiritual house who offer spiritual sacrifices, interpreting sanctuary and offering through a community.
Believers are built into a spiritual house and holy priesthood to offer spiritual sacrifices, fusing house, communal belonging, and worship.

basis: betrothed and presented to one husband
note: Paul says he betrothed the community to one husband in order to present it as a pure virgin to Christ, directly recasting bride-transfer in ecclesial terms.
The author praises faithful service to brothers who are strangers, a concrete Christian mandate to receive travelling outsiders.
The travelling brothers go out for the sake of the Name while taking nothing from outsiders, relating hospitality to named religious mission.
The commentary links an offering with nearness to God and a gift with care for another; the angel tells Cornelius that his prayers and alms have risen as a memorial before God.

basis: relief gift for a distant community
note: The disciples determine to send relief to the brothers living in Judea, an actual communal gift conveyed to people in need.
The relief is sent to the elders through Barnabas and Saul, preserving the physical mediation of a gift's journey to its recipients.

basis: prisoners welcomed into the jailer's house
note: The jailer brings Paul and Silas into his house and sets food before them after their release, converting a scene of custody and fear into domestic welcome.

basis: alms and offerings brought after travel
note: Paul says that after years away he came to bring alms for his nation and offerings, directly joining travel, gift, and cultic act.
After shipwreck, the islanders show unusual kindness and kindle a fire for all the survivors, a narrative of emergency welcome.

basis: shipwrecked travelers received into a house
note: Publius receives Paul and the shipwrecked party and entertains them for three days, an explicit house-based shelter for travellers.

basis: a traveler asks for a guide
note: The commentary's ihdinā is a request for guidance; the Ethiopian traveler asks how he can understand Isaiah unless someone guides him, and Philip joins him on the road.

The commentary's hedy is an animal led to a sacred destination; Acts quotes Isaiah's sheep led to slaughter in Philip's explanation of Jesus, making the sacrificial animal a Christian reading of a human figure.
Ephesians names Gentiles as aliens from Israel and strangers to the covenants; it gives the exclusion from which the commentary's asylum-and-covenant image moves.
Those once strangers and aliens become fellow citizens and members of God's household, an unusually direct Christian counterpart to secure communal belonging.

The commentary defines a gift as kindness sent to someone loved and the hedy as an offering for nearness to God; Ephesians says Christ loved people and gave himself as an offering and sacrifice to God.

basis: the bride presented to the husband
note: The commentary says the bride is gathered to her husband; Ephesians reads marriage as Christ presenting the church to himself, a Christian interpretation that turns the household image into Christ and church.
Christ presents the church to himself in splendor; the marital image supplies the end-point of a bride brought to her husband.

basis: entry into holy place through sacrifice
note: Believers have confidence to enter the holy places by Jesus' blood; sacrifice here grants access to the sacred destination.
The access of the preceding verse is described as a new and living way, explicitly making sacrificial approach a path.
The commentary says guidance has a home at the end of its road; Hebrews describes travelers seeking a better homeland and a city God has prepared for them.
The faithful seek a better, heavenly country, and God has prepared a city for them; pilgrimage toward a divinely prepared home is explicit.
Believers have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, expressing the destination as an already approached heavenly sanctuary.
The commentary's hedy is brought to the House as an offering; Hebrews describes sacrificial animals whose blood the high priest brings into the holy place while their bodies are burned outside camp.
The commentary's animal reaches the sacred House; Hebrews says Jesus suffered outside the city gate and sanctified people by his blood, relocating the Christian sacrifice beyond the city.
Christians have no lasting city here but seek the city that is coming, a compact formulation of road-like yearning for final belonging.
The commentary joins sacrifice, worship, and the name spoken over the animal; Hebrews calls praise a sacrifice to God and the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name.

basis: sacrifice of praise and confession of Name
note: Through Jesus believers offer continual praise to God, identified as lips confessing his name; name and sacrifice are made verbal rather than animal.
The commentary calls a gift an act of kindness to someone loved; Hebrews says doing good and sharing resources are sacrifices pleasing to God.
The commentary's asylum seeker asks a group for shelter or a pledge; Hebrews describes people who fled for refuge to seize hope grounded in God's unchangeable promise and oath.
The author speaks of people who have fled for refuge to hold fast hope; an asylum image is used directly, even though its meaning is theological.
Hope enters the inner place behind the curtain, carrying the refuge image into access to God's sanctuary rather than a secular shelter.
Christ's death mediates a new covenant so those called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, relating sacrifice to secure belonging rather than an animal's arrival.

basis: sheep called by name and led
note: The commentary says God's name is uttered over the hedy and the animal is taken toward its destination; Jesus' shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, though here the sheep are living followers.

basis: shepherd calls by name and leads sheep
note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out; animal, name, and guidance are joined, though the sheep are not sacrificial offerings.
Whoever enters through Jesus is saved and finds pasture; the doorway turns guidance into safety and sustenance rather than a Temple destination.

basis: a costly gift offered to a beloved guest
note: The commentary defines a gift as kindness sent to someone cherished; Mary pours costly perfume on Jesus at a meal, and he defends her act as appropriate to his burial.
Mary pours costly perfume on Jesus in a house, a concrete gift of devotion whose domestic setting and beloved recipient recall the commentary's gift image.
The commentary says the guided path has a house at its end; Jesus promises his disciples many dwelling places in his Father's house.
Jesus describes his Father's house as having many dwelling places, giving the prayer for guidance an explicitly eschatological house as destination.

basis: the guide takes people to himself
note: The commentary's bride reaches her husband's home and the refugee his safe place; Jesus promises to come and take his followers to himself so they can be where he is.
Jesus promises to come again and take his followers to himself so that they may be where he is, turning destination into belonging with a person.
Jesus calls himself the way to the Father; the Christian text personalizes the path whose end is the Father's house in the same discourse.
Jesus says he guarded his followers in the Father's name and none was lost except the designated exception; the name is presented as protective custody.

basis: the Passover rule read through Jesus
note: The commentary's hedy is an animal designated for sacrifice; John interprets Jesus' unbroken bones through the Passover lamb rule, extending the animal offering image to his death.

The commentary labels Arabic rabb as Lord and reports a covenant-related branch; Mary calls the risen Jesus Rabbouni, an Aramaic honorific meaning teacher or master, supporting the address sense rather than covenant.
John calls the bride the bridegroom's and identifies the listening friend who rejoices at his voice; bride, husband, and friend are explicitly differentiated.

basis: worship no longer tied to either mountain
note: The commentary follows the hedy to the Haram and the old House; Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that the hour comes when worship will be neither on her mountain nor in Jerusalem.

The commentary locates the sacrificial animal's destination at a sacred House; Jesus describes the coming worship as in spirit and truth, shifting attention from a sanctuary site to the worshippers' manner.
The commentary's ihdinā asks to be led on a path; Zechariah says the dawn from on high will guide people's feet into the way of peace.
Zacharias says God's dawn will guide feet into the way of peace, a focused New Testament articulation of the prayer for guidance without the house image.
The Samaritan puts the wounded man on his own animal, brings him to an inn, and cares for him, a notably close scene of transport into safety.
The commentary's hedy animal is carried from a flock toward the House; Jesus' parable has a shepherd carry a recovered sheep on his shoulders, turning the journey into rescue rather than sacrifice.
After finding the sheep, the shepherd puts it on his shoulders rejoicing; this is the carrying action that culminates in the homecoming already represented by the next verse.
The commentary hears ihdinā as a road that reaches home; the shepherd returns with the sheep and calls friends and neighbors together to celebrate.
The shepherd comes home with the recovered sheep and calls friends and neighbors to rejoice; return, animal, home, and friendship meet in the parable.

basis: a family brings a child to the sanctuary
note: The commentary's route ends at a sacred House; Luke has Jesus' parents bring him to Jerusalem for presentation and purification under the Law.
Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, a New Testament movement of a person toward the holy place for cultic presentation.

basis: two birds offered at the sanctuary
note: The commentary describes livestock carried to a sacred destination; Luke specifies the poor family's pair of doves or pigeons as the offering brought with Jesus to the Temple.
The couple offers the prescribed birds at the Temple; this supplies the animal-offering side of the Jerusalem presentation scene.

basis: the path is prepared for the Lord
note: The commentary's prayer asks God to guide worshippers on the straight way; Mark applies Isaiah's road formula to John preparing the Lord's way, reversing who is guided and who comes.

basis: Queen of the South as witness
note: The commentary's Queen of Sheba sends Solomon a gift that he rejects; Matthew remembers her journey from earth's ends to hear Solomon and makes her a witness against Jesus' generation, adding a judgment interpretation.

basis: gift delivered to a child in a house
note: The commentary describes a gift carried to its recipient and contrasts the rejected gift to Solomon; the Magi enter a house, worship the child, and present him gifts that are received.
The magi enter a house, worship the child, and open their treasures; destination, reverence, and a carried gift converge without requiring the gift to be a sacrifice.
The commentary describes a petitioner seeking protection and a safe destination; Joseph takes the child and mother to Egypt to escape Herod's threat.
An angel directs Joseph to take the child and mother and flee to Egypt from lethal danger, a New Testament journey of protected asylum.
Joseph takes the child and mother by night and withdraws to Egypt, giving the refugee movement itself its own narrative verse.
The angel tells Joseph to take the child and mother back to Israel because the threat has died; refuge ends in a guided return home.

basis: a star guides travelers to a house
note: The commentary says guidance carries its subject to a destination; the Magi follow the star until it stands over the place where the child is.
The star goes ahead of the magi until it stands over the place of the child, a guided journey that has a precise domestic destination.

basis: going out to meet the bridegroom
note: The virgins take lamps and go out to meet the bridegroom, supplying the journey-to-wedding aspect whose arrival is described later in the parable.
The prepared virgins go with the bridegroom into the wedding feast and the door is shut, portraying a completed movement into a wedding household.
Those judged righteous say they gathered in a stranger; the concrete act of receiving an outsider gives a Christian household analogue to the protected arrival.

basis: gift at altar and reconciled relation
note: Jesus' altar saying makes the acceptability of a gift depend on repairing a broken relation first, a relevant contrast to the commentary's distinction between gift to friend and to rival.
God highly exalts Jesus and grants the name above every name after the obedient self-giving of the preceding verse, a close Christian analogue to raised name and obedient service.
The commentary describes a gift as kindness sent to someone loved; Paul calls the Philippians' material gift a fragrant offering and acceptable sacrifice to God.
Paul calls the Philippians' material gift a fragrant, acceptable sacrifice pleasing to God, combining an affectional gift with sacrificial language.

basis: receive a contested person as oneself
note: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul; without assuming Onesimus's legal status, the verse makes personal welcome the requested resolution.
The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with people bearing his and his Father's name on their foreheads, binding Name, mark, and sacred destination.
The marriage of the Lamb comes and his bride has made herself ready, a final wedding scene that gives the bridal route an eschatological destination.

basis: invited to the Lamb's marriage supper
note: The blessed are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb, giving the bridal arrival a communal table and final welcome.

basis: the bride is a descending city
note: The commentary's bride is carried to her husband's home; Revelation pictures the holy city descending from heaven adorned as a bride, reversing the direction and making the bride a city.
New Jerusalem descends prepared as a bride adorned for her husband; city-home and bride are deliberately merged in one arrival image.

basis: glory and honor brought into the city
note: The glory and honor of nations are brought into New Jerusalem, an eschatological analogue to gifts conveyed into the sacred home.
The commentary imagines the path ending at a home; Revelation says God's dwelling is with humanity, making the destination a shared divine-human home.
The divine dwelling is among human beings and they are God's people, providing the final communal home sought in the commentary's road image.

basis: servants worship in the final city
note: In the renewed city God's servants worship him; permanent dwelling and service meet after the removal of the curse.
The servants see God's face and bear his name on their foreheads, completing the New Testament line of name as identity and protection.
The victor becomes a permanent pillar in God's temple and bears God's name and the name of the new Jerusalem, combining inviolability, house, and name.
The commentary joins the hedy animal with the request for guidance toward a safe destination; Revelation's Lamb becomes shepherd and guides the protected multitude to springs of living water.
Revelation's Lamb shepherds and guides people to springs of living water; it reverses the commentary's guided sacrificial animal into an animal figure that guides others.
Angels are told not to harm land or sea until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads; a visible divine mark creates temporary inviolability.

basis: only the unsealed may be harmed
note: The destructive creatures may harm only those lacking God's seal on their foreheads, continuing the marked-protection pattern with an explicit exclusion.
Believers present their bodies as a living sacrifice, which Paul calls worship; it explicitly joins sacrifice with the service dimension the commentary draws from عبادت.
Macedonia and Achaia make a contribution for poor saints in Jerusalem, a Christian gift carried toward a named communal home.
Pesahim contrasts Abraham's mountain and Isaac's field with Jacob's name for the future sanctuary as a house, sharpening the commentary's claim that sacred approach ends at a home.

basis: God leads the restored people with joy
note: Baruch says God will lead Israel in joy by the light of his glory with mercy and righteousness; its restoration context supplies a later Jewish guided-homecoming image.
The midrash depicts God as acting as Adam's bridal attendant when he brings Eve to him, explicitly elaborating Genesis's bride-transfer scene.
Midrash on the Akedah identifies Moriah with the later sanctuary, reading Abraham's sacrificial journey as oriented toward the place that becomes God's house.

This Mekhilta discussion is commonly cited as reading Exodus 15's holy dwelling and sanctuary in Temple terms; the exact wording and subdivision should be verified, but its interpretive bridge is sacrifice's destination as God's house.
The first-fruit towns assemble and ascend toward Zion in procession; it is a Jewish ritual realization of a marked gathering traveling with gifts to God's place.
The Mishnah describes first fruits borne in baskets and handed to priests, a precise Jewish counterpart to the commentary's carried gift and its tray.
The Mishnah makes appearance at the pilgrimage festivals an obligation with an offering, preserving the gathered-season and carried-sacrifice pattern as law.
The Mishnah describes roads marked 'refuge, refuge' toward the cities of refuge; it makes the road itself visibly direct a fleeing person toward safety.
High priests' mothers supply food and clothing to accidental killers in refuge cities, treating arrival at refuge as an ongoing protected residence.

The commentary places marriage before the bride's journey; this mishna frames betrothal as a legal act through money, document, or intercourse, clarifying the formal bond preceding full household union.
The Mishnah opens by saying that a woman is acquired in three ways; it gives a Jewish legal frame for the commentary's marriage language in the malik family.
The Mishnah says that after Jerusalem was chosen, high places were forbidden permanently; it interprets sacrifice as bound to its final house.

basis: pilgrims form a common sacred homeland
note: Philo describes festival pilgrims leaving their local places for the Temple and recovering a common kinship there; the cited section should be checked, but it is a specific Hellenistic-Jewish expansion of travel into sacred home.
The Targum renders Ruth's refuge as taking shelter under the wings of the Shekinah, making her foreign arrival an explicitly Jewish covenantal shelter image.

basis: nations bring gifts to God's Name
note: Tobit's hymn foresees nations coming from afar with gifts in hand for the heavenly king because of the Lord's name, combining pilgrimage, gift, and exalted name.

basis: bride directed to her husband's family home
note: The commentary's bride is conveyed to her husband's house; Raguel gives Sarah to Tobias and directs him to take her to his father's house. Tobit's verse numbering varies among editions.
The congregation is told to ascribe glory to YHWH's name, bring an offering, and come before him; elevated name and conveyed offering share one command.

basis: house and altar of burnt offering
note: David identifies the future site as both God's house and the altar of burnt offering for Israel, an exact house-and-sacrifice formulation.
Adonijah fears Solomon and takes hold of the altar's horns, using sacred space and its object as a claim to protection.
The commentary says the Qur'anic queen's gift to Solomon fails to reach him; Kings narrates the same queen giving him abundant gold, spices, and stones as a successful royal exchange.
The queen gives Solomon gold, spices, and precious stones; Kings narrates the transfer without Solomon's Qur'anic rebuff of the gift.
The commentary's Sheba scene ends with Solomon dismissing the gift; Kings says he gave the queen whatever she desired and royal gifts in return.
Kings has Solomon give the queen all she desired in addition to royal gifts, making reciprocal exchange rather than rejection the outcome of the parallel royal encounter.
The Queen of Sheba herself comes to Solomon with a camel caravan and wealth, whereas the Qur'anic scene developed in the commentary has the queen send a gift before meeting him.

basis: call on a god's name at a bull altar
note: The commentary joins the offered animal with the name spoken over it; at Carmel, two bulls are prepared and each side calls on its god's name, in a test that contrasts YHWH with Baal.
The commentary says a person who seeks a group's protection becomes inviolable like the House's offering; Joab flees to YHWH's altar and grips its horns for sanctuary.

basis: altar refuge does not save Joab
note: The commentary presents the asylum seeker as protected like a sacred offering; after Joab takes refuge at the altar, Solomon's men execute him, showing that this sanctuary's protection can fail.

basis: foreigner comes from afar for the Name
note: Solomon imagines a foreigner hearing of YHWH's great name and coming from a distant country, a pilgrimage of an outsider toward the named house.
God is asked to hear the foreigner who prays toward the Temple so all peoples know his name; house, name, and outsider access are explicitly related.

basis: a child and offerings brought to God's house
note: The commentary describes an animal carried to a sacred house; Hannah brings Samuel, a bull, flour, and wine to YHWH's house at Shiloh, dedicating the child rather than sacrificing him.

basis: a person given to divine service
note: The commentary links a subdued animal with service and worship; Hannah says she gives Samuel to YHWH for all his days, a human dedication at the sanctuary.
Samuel says obedience and listening are better than sacrifice and rams' fat; this directly challenges any reading in which the guided animal itself exhausts worship.
Abigail loads food gifts onto donkeys and takes them to David during a dangerous encounter; it is a carried gift aimed at a potentially hostile recipient.
Abigail calls the gift she has brought David a blessing, supplying a biblical way in which a conveyed present is spoken of as benefit.
The commentary says a gift sent to a rival does not reach Solomon; Abigail's gift reaches David, who accepts it and abandons his plan to kill Nabal's household.
The commentary's petitioner asks a group for protection and a pledge; the Egyptian slave asks David to swear not to kill or return him before he agrees to guide the pursuit.
Chronicles places Solomon's Temple on Mount Moriah, canonically joining the shown sacrificial mountain to the later house of worship.
God's choice of Jerusalem for his name makes the temple city a named destination, supplementing the commentary's stress on a house reached through worship.
God calls the chosen Temple site a house of sacrifice, an unusually direct biblical pairing of house and sacrificial destination.

basis: a prophet refuses a foreigner's gift
note: The commentary says Solomon rejects Sheba's gift; Elisha refuses Naaman's gift after healing him, showing a different reason a sacred figure will not accept a valuable present.

basis: rejected offerings at a hated festival
note: God says he will not accept offerings or regard peace offerings in a prophetic critique of cult; it counterbalances the commentary's festival sacrifice with the ethical conditions of acceptance.

The commentary labels Arabic rabb as Lord but also reports a separate covenant sense; Daniel's Aramaic rab names Daniel chief of the governors, supporting the rank or master sense rather than the covenant gloss.
The commentary's hedy animal reaches the House; Deuteronomy sends burnt offerings and other gifts to the place YHWH chooses to establish his name.
Israel must bring its offerings to the place YHWH chooses for his name to dwell, directly linking name, sacred house, and transported sacrifices.

Arabic ism in بِسْمِ and Hebrew shem are cognate name terms; Deuteronomy uses shem for the divine name dwelling where offerings are brought, while the commentary's listed س م و label is not being treated as proof.

basis: seeking the place of the Name
note: Israel is commanded to seek the place YHWH chooses for his name and dwelling; the verb of seeking makes pilgrimage toward the house explicit.

basis: journey too long to carry the gift
note: Deuteronomy considers the practical case in which the chosen place is too far for someone to carry the tithe, a precise biblical reflection on a religious gift in transit.
Firstborn animals from herd and flock are eaten before YHWH year by year at the chosen place, combining animal, pilgrimage, and household celebration.
The household rejoices at the place where YHWH causes his name to dwell together with Levite, resident alien, orphan, and widow; seasonal gathering includes vulnerable outsiders.
At the three annual appearances before God, no one is to appear empty-handed; seasonal gathering, journey to the chosen place, and carried gift form one obligation.
Each pilgrim gives according to the blessing YHWH has given, a concrete biblical joining of gift, pilgrimage, and received benefit.
The Passover sacrifice is taken from flock or herd and offered at the place YHWH chooses for his name to dwell, closely matching animal, house, and named worship.

basis: a fugitive slave given a safe dwelling
note: The commentary's outsider asks a group for protection and reaches a safe place; Deuteronomy says an escaped slave may live where he chooses among Israel and must not be oppressed.
The community may not hand an escaped slave back to his master, a direct rule against returning a person who has sought safety.
The escaped slave may live among the community in the place he chooses and must not be oppressed; protection is completed by a chosen home.

basis: gift set before God and worshiped
note: The first fruits are brought and set before YHWH, followed by worship; gift delivery becomes an act of devotion at the sacred destination.

basis: basket of first fruits to chosen place
note: The worshiper takes first fruits in a basket and goes to the place YHWH chooses for his name; this is unusually close to the commentary's tray-borne gift.
God promises to gather Israel even from the ends of heaven, a return movement for people who are dispersed and outside their secure place.
God brings the gathered people back into the land of their ancestors and makes them possess it, making return culminate in a home and inheritance.
The commentary glosses Arabic ʿibāda as obedience and service; Deuteronomy uses the Hebrew cognate ʿābad for serving YHWH, alongside cleaving to him and swearing by his name.
Israel is to fear and serve YHWH and swear by his name; Hebrew עבד supplies a cognate service context alongside the commentary's name-and-worship connection.
Esther is taken to the king in his royal palace, a courtly version of a woman being conveyed into a husband's household.

basis: Arabic م ل ك and Hebrew מלך
note: Hebrew melek, cognate with the source's مٰلِك family, means king here; Esther's actual transfer to the king's palace gives a concrete royal-marital setting without equating the two traditions' marriage vocabulary.

basis: blood as a sign protecting a house
note: The commentary connects a mark or sign with the gathered season and describes the refuge-seeker as protected; Passover blood is a sign on households that protects them from the destroying plague.
Blood serves as a sign on Israelite houses and causes the plague to pass over; a mark makes a dwelling and those inside it inviolable.
The Passover sacrifice belongs to YHWH who passed over Israelite houses; sacrifice, named worship, household, and protection meet in one rite.

basis: a lamb selected for each household
note: The commentary describes a sacrificial animal separated from a herd and taken toward a sacred destination; Passover assigns a lamb to each household, with a different destination and purpose.
YHWH goes before Israel in cloud and fire to lead them on the way, an explicit wilderness model for divine direction.
Exodus says God led the redeemed people by strength to his holy abode; it supplies a scriptural journey whose end is a dwelling, the completion the commentary hears in ihdinā.
Following the holy-dwelling line, the song says God will bring and plant his people at the mountain of his inheritance, the place made for his dwelling and sanctuary.
God says he bore Israel on eagles' wings and brought them to himself; divine conveyance creates the covenantal nearness sought in the commentary.

The commentary labels bismi with Arabic roots s-m-w and w-s-m and says the uttered name raises remembrance of its bearer; Hebrew shem is remembered at an altar where burnt and peace offerings are made.
God permits an altar for animal offerings and promises to come and bless wherever he causes his name to be remembered; this directly joins sacrifice, name, and divine approach.

basis: a place of refuge for accidental killing
note: The commentary describes a person accepted under protection; Exodus says God provides a place to which the unintended killer may flee.
God appoints a place to which an accidental killer may flee, a foundational legal scene of flight toward secured space.
The commentary calls the petitioner inviolable like the House's offering; Exodus orders even an intentional killer taken from God's altar and put to death, defining a limit to sanctuary protection.

basis: altar refuge has a legal limit
note: Exodus orders a presumptuous murderer taken even from God's altar; against the commentary's inviolable protected person, this marks the Torah's stated limit on sanctuary asylum.
The commentary's mawsim is a marked season of gathering; Exodus fixes an appointed feast and says no one should appear before God empty-handed.
God sends an angel to guard Israel on the way and bring them to a prepared place, combining escort, safety, and a divinely assigned destination.

basis: Arabic ع ب د and Hebrew עבד
note: The commentary's ع ب د label and Hebrew עבד are cognate service terms; Exodus has Israel serve God on the mountain after deliverance, without importing the commentary's camel sense into Hebrew.
God promises that no one will covet Israel's land while its males go up for the three pilgrimage festivals; travel to worship is placed under explicit protection.

basis: first fruits brought to God's house
note: The first of the land's produce must be brought into the house of YHWH, a compact Torah model for a gift physically conveyed to the sacred home.
The commentary separately develops a refugee receiving protection and a bride joined to her husband; Ezekiel's allegory has YHWH cover Jerusalem, swear a covenant, and claim her as his wife.
God covers Jerusalem, swears an oath, enters covenant, and says she became his; the prophetic marriage image makes covenant the act that establishes belonging.
On God's holy mountain Israel will serve him and bring offerings, first fruits, and holy gifts; destination, service, and conveyed gift all appear in one verse.
God makes an everlasting covenant of peace, multiplies the people, and sets his sanctuary among them; covenant becomes enduring protected proximity.
God's dwelling is with the people, and he is their God while they are his people; the final home is reciprocal belonging.
Resident aliens who live among Israel and have children there receive inheritance among the tribes; protection reaches the level of a permanent home.

basis: right way for people and possessions
note: Ezra proclaims a fast to seek from God a right way for the returning people, their children, and their property, a concrete prayer for safeguarded travel.
God's hand delivers the returning caravan from enemy and ambush on the way, giving the safe-route element a historical narrative form.
The transported silver, gold, and vessels are weighed in the house of God at Jerusalem; a carried offering demonstrably reaches its sacred recipient.
The lights serve for signs and appointed seasons; this is a specific biblical pairing for the commentary's marked season, though it is cosmic rather than pilgrimage law.
God forms the woman and brings her to the man, a concise biblical scene of a bride being led to her husband.

basis: leaving one household to join another
note: The commentary's bride is gathered to her husband; Genesis describes the marital bond as leaving father and mother and cleaving to one's wife.

basis: ram offered instead of a son
note: The commentary's hedy is an animal carried to a sacred destination; Abraham offers a ram as a burnt offering instead of Isaac, making the animal a substitute for a beloved child.
The ram caught at Moriah is offered in Isaac's place, giving the selected mountain an actual animal offering within the Akedah scene.
Abraham is told to go to Moriah and offer on a mountain God will show him, a sacrifice directed toward a disclosed destination rather than offered anywhere.

basis: blessing expressed in herds and camels
note: Abraham's blessing is narrated as flocks, herds, wealth, servants, camels, and donkeys; it illuminates the commentary's association of received benefit with herd animals and the bridal camel journey.
The servant gives Rebekah ornaments and gives precious things to her kin, a gift-bearing scene embedded in the transfer of a bride.
Rebekah and her attendants mount camels and follow Abraham's servant, beginning a bridal journey with the animal explicitly named in the commentary.

basis: bride brought to the husband's tent
note: The commentary describes the bride being taken to her husband's home; Isaac brings Rebekah into his mother's tent and takes her as his wife.
Isaac brings Rebekah into Sarah's tent and takes her as wife; the bridal journey ends in incorporation into the husband's household.

basis: house of God and gate of heaven
note: Jacob calls Bethel the house of God and the gate of heaven; it gives the commentary's final home a threshold where earthly travel meets divine presence.
Jacob's vow asks God to be with him and guard him on the way he travels, a direct individual counterpart to a request for guidance with protection.

basis: bayt and bayit: journey to a father's house
note: The commentary glosses hidaya as showing the way and the house at its end; Jacob asks to return in peace to his father's bayit, the Hebrew cognate of Arabic bayt, after his journey.

basis: return in peace to father's house
note: Jacob seeks to return safely to his father's house; the goal of the guarded road is explicitly a home and restored belonging.

basis: bayt and bayit: a sacred house
note: The commentary's route ends at the House; Jacob names the place where he slept Bet-El, God's house, using the Hebrew cognate of Arabic bayt for a sanctuary.
The Bethel stone is to become God's house, and Jacob vows a tithe from what God gives him; sacred dwelling and conveyed gift are conjoined.
Laban brings Leah to Jacob at night; the same transfer scene appears here within a deceptive marriage narrative, which keeps the relation from being idealized.
Jacob selects a gift for Esau before their feared meeting, an actual gift sent ahead to repair a dangerous relationship.
The commentary says a gift sent to a rival may fail to reach its recipient; Jacob presses Esau to accept a gift after their estrangement, presenting it as a sign of God's favor and reconciliation.
Jacob asks Esau to accept his blessing, meaning the present sent ahead; a gift between estranged kin is thus expressed through blessing language.

basis: go to Bethel, dwell, and build altar
note: God tells Jacob to arise, go to Bethel, dwell there, and make an altar; route, settlement, and sacrificial worship are inseparable instructions.
Jacob says God answered him in distress and was with him on the way, then calls his household to go build an altar at Bethel.
Jacob builds an altar at Bethel and names the place El-Bethel, making arrival at God's house culminate in sacrificial action.

basis: protective sign on a vulnerable person
note: God puts a sign on Cain so that no one who finds him will kill him; it is a marked person's inviolability, though not an asylum treaty.
Abel brings firstborn animals from his flock and their fat portions, and YHWH regards him and his offering; animal gift and acceptance are explicit.
Cain's offering is not regarded, providing another scriptural instance in which the relation between giver and recipient, rather than conveyance alone, determines an offering's reception.

basis: gifts carried to a powerful unknown recipient
note: Jacob sends his sons with choice products as a present to the Egyptian ruler, a carried gift aimed at a recipient whose disposition is uncertain.
The commentary describes a person arriving among a group and seeking protection; Isaiah calls for Moab to hide outcasts and not betray fugitives.
The appeal asks Judah to provide shade like night and hide the outcasts, a vivid shelter image for endangered arrivals.

basis: the refugee lives in a hiding place
note: The commentary's petitioner is protected by the community he approaches; Isaiah asks Moab to let Judah's outcasts dwell there as shelter from the destroyer.
The speaker asks that Moab's outcasts live with Judah and that Judah be a shelter from the destroyer, closely matching asylum in another community.
A gift or tribute is brought to the place of the name of YHWH on Zion, giving a biblical destination for a carried offering.
The commentary pictures guidance whose path ends at a sacred home; Isaiah has peoples go up to YHWH's mountain to learn his ways and walk in his paths.
Nations go up to the house of Jacob's God so that he may teach them his ways and they may walk his paths; house and guided way are one scene.

The commentary's explicit Beyt or house image corresponds formally to Hebrew bêt in 'house of the God of Jacob'; the verse's actual context supplies ascent and taught paths, not a lexical claim alone.
The commentary's worshippers ask God to guide them along a straight path; Isaiah instead commands a wilderness voice to prepare a straight highway for YHWH's own coming.
God brings foreign adherents to his holy mountain; their offerings are accepted on his altar in a house of prayer, bringing outsider reception and sacrifice together.

basis: homeless poor brought into one's house
note: Isaiah defines righteous care in part as bringing the homeless poor into one's house, an exact home-making act for a vulnerable outsider.
Camels carry gold and frankincense to Zion while proclaiming YHWH's praise, a caravan image that joins the commentary's camels, carried gift, and exalted name.

basis: flocks on altar and glorified house
note: Flocks are accepted on God's altar and he glorifies his house; this makes herd animals reach the sanctuary for worship.
God leads the returning people by streams on a straight path where they will not stumble; it gives a prophetic form of safe guidance, though the verse names no house.

basis: displaced people ask for a way
note: The commentary reads ihdinā as asking for a route that reaches safety; Judah's remnant asks Jeremiah to seek God's direction about the way they should go after Jerusalem's fall.
Job says no stranger had to lodge in the street because he opened his doors to the traveler, a domestic counterpart to sheltering the one who arrives.
The commentary's refugee asks a group for protection or a pledge; Rahab asks the Israelite spies to swear that they will spare her family because she has shown them loyalty.
The commentary links refuge with a protective covenant; the spies swear to preserve Rahab's life if she keeps their mission secret.

basis: admission and a place to dwell
note: A fugitive reaches the city gate, states his case to elders, is admitted, and receives a place to live among them; this is especially close to the commentary's seeker of protection.
Joshua's 'my house will serve YHWH' uses Hebrew עבד, cognate with the commentary's عبادت family, and locates worshipful service within a household declaration.
Rahab and her family are spared and she dwells in Israel because of the oath-bound protection she gave the spies; asylum, covenant, and communal incorporation coincide.
The commentary links an asylum-seeker with a pledge from the group; Joshua makes peace and a covenant with Gibeon, letting its people live.
Joshua makes peace with the Gibeonites, makes a covenant, and leaders swear to them; a community's word creates their protected status.
The commentary says the protected petitioner becomes inviolable; Israel does not strike the Gibeonites because its leaders swore an oath to them.
The leaders say the sworn oath prevents the congregation from striking the Gibeonites, showing the protective force of a covenantal promise.

The commentary explicitly says the hedy is brought as qurbah, nearness to God; Leviticus uses Hebrew qorban for an offering from herd or flock brought to YHWH, a cognate word family in a concrete sacrificial setting.

basis: herd or flock animal brought to YHWH
note: The commentary describes the hedy as an animal taken from a herd to the Haram; Leviticus likewise tells the worshipper to bring an offering from herd or flock to YHWH, while its cultic destination is the tent.

basis: herd animal brought to the entrance
note: The commentary's hedy is taken from a herd to a sacred destination; Leviticus prescribes a male animal without blemish brought to the tent entrance as a voluntary burnt offering.
A voluntary herd burnt offering is brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting for acceptance before YHWH, giving a more formal sacrificial arrival scene.
The commentary calls the hedy an offering for nearness to God; Leviticus says the offerer lays a hand on the animal's head so it may be accepted to make atonement.
An ox, lamb, or goat slaughtered for sacrifice must be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting before YHWH; the animal's holy use depends on reaching the appointed place.
The commentary describes an animal carried to the Haram for offering; Leviticus requires Israelites to bring oxen, lambs, or goats to the tent entrance as offerings to YHWH.
The mo'adim are YHWH's appointed times and holy convocations, a calendrical gathering marked out in a way comparable to the commentary's season-sign.

The commentary says a protected petitioner has hurma like the House's hedy; Hebrew ḥerem here is irrevocably devoted to YHWH and unavailable for ordinary sale, a cognate with a related consecration sense rather than the same sanctuary meaning.
God says he will not accept an offering from the speakers' hand; it supplies a different reason for an offered gift to fail to reach its intended acceptance.
The commentary brings the hedy offering together with God's name and the worlds; Malachi pictures nations from sunrise to sunset offering incense and a pure gift to YHWH's name.
The prophetic vision of incense and a pure offering for YHWH's great name gives the name-and-offering conjunction developed in the commentary.

basis: male from flock and great Name
note: Malachi contrasts a vowed male animal withheld from sacrifice with YHWH's great name among nations, directly coupling flock, offering, and name.
Malachi calls the wife a partner and wife of covenant, giving a concise biblical equation of marriage with a binding protective relationship.
The ark goes before Israel to seek out a resting place, a covenantal guide moving the people toward a place where they may settle.
Israel camps by standards and signs of ancestral houses around the Tent; marked communal gathering around a dwelling gives a concrete analogue to the season-as-sign image.
The commentary's petitioner seeks a group's protection and a safe destination; Numbers appoints cities to which an accidental killer may flee from the blood-avenger.
Israel designates cities of refuge so that a manslayer may flee there; refuge is reached by travel to a named communal place.
The refuge cities are for Israelites, resident aliens, and sojourners, making protected arrival available across communal status.

basis: God's name placed on a people
note: The commentary says God's name is spoken over the hedy animal; this priestly formula places YHWH's name over Israel and promises blessing, applying the ritual name to the protected community.
God says the priests place his name on Israel and he blesses them; the name functions as a bearer of benefit rather than merely an utterance over an animal.

basis: gift opens access to the great
note: A person's gift makes room for him and brings him before great people, a concise wisdom-text account of a gift as mediated access to a recipient.

basis: straight road to a settled city
note: The commentary hears ihdinā as a request to reach the home at the path's end; these desert wanderers are led by YHWH on a straight route until they reach an inhabited city.
God leads wilderness wanderers by a straight way until they reach a city to inhabit; the verse makes a straight road culminate in a place of belonging.

basis: sacrifice and invocation of the name
note: The commentary says God's name is spoken over the hedy and links it to worship; the psalmist offers a thanksgiving sacrifice while calling on YHWH's name.
The worshiper offers a thanksgiving sacrifice and calls on YHWH's name, an explicit analogue to sacrifice accompanied by divine naming.
The commentary's path reaches a House and its season gathers people; the psalmist fulfills vows in the courts of YHWH's house amid Jerusalem's assembly.
The commentary joins a name spoken over an offering with arrival at the House; this pilgrimage greeting blesses the person who comes in YHWH's name to the sanctuary.

basis: festal offering brought to the altar
note: The commentary's animal must reach its sacrificial destination; this verse is often read as binding the festal offering to the altar horns, though the Hebrew phrase's referent is disputed.
The commentary connects mawsim with a gathering and the House; here tribes go up to Jerusalem as Israel's testimony to give thanks to YHWH's name.
The commentary says ihdinā asks to be brought beyond the road toward its home; this speaker asks light and truth to guide him and bring him to God's holy mountain and dwelling.
The psalm asks that God's light and truth lead the speaker and bring him to God's holy hill and dwellings, closely joining guidance with arrival at a sacred home.
The commentary reads h-d-y as a bride conducted to her husband's home; this royal wedding psalm says the princess is led to the king with companions following her.
The commentary's bride is brought to her husband's house; the next wedding verse has the bridal party enter the king's palace with joy.
The commentary says the spoken name raises remembrance of the named one; this wedding psalm promises that the king's name will be remembered through generations.
The commentary's Arabic malik names God as sovereign; the Hebrew cognate melekh here declares God king over all the earth, while the commentary's marriage gloss remains a separate Arabic branch.

basis: thanksgiving sacrifice and a rightly ordered way
note: The commentary joins worship, offering, and the request for guidance; this psalm says a thanksgiving sacrifice honors God and that the one who orders his way rightly will see God's salvation.

basis: a flock led through the wilderness
note: The commentary joins an animal from a herd with divine guidance; this psalm says YHWH led Israel like sheep and guided them through the wilderness like a flock.
The commentary pictures the guided route ending at a sacred home; the psalm says God brought the flock to the border of his sanctuary, to the mountain he claimed.
The commentary itself labels Arabic anʿamta, favor, and anʿām, herds, under n-ʿ-m; Hebrew noam here means YHWH's gracious pleasantness, a possible cognate for the favor sense but not for livestock.
The worshiper is told to ascribe glory to YHWH's name, bring an offering, and come into his courts, a close formulaic counterpart to the commentary's named animal and house.
The commentary describes an outsider seeking a group's safe protection; Boaz blesses Ruth for coming to take refuge under YHWH's wings.
Boaz says Ruth has come to seek refuge under YHWH's wings after leaving her own people; it is a personal migration into protected covenantal belonging.
Boaz says that he has acquired Ruth as wife; it is a biblical legal idiom in which marriage is expressed through acquisition, relevant to the commentary's imlāk image.
The commentary develops refuge and a bride brought to her husband's home; Ruth first seeks refuge as a foreigner, then marries Boaz and joins his household.
The speaker says the king has brought her into his chambers, a concise bridal arrival image in which the groom's dwelling is the destination.
The woman says she would lead her beloved into her mother's house; its reversed direction and household make it a useful contrary bride-and-home image.
God brings scattered people to dwell in Jerusalem, and they become his people while he becomes their God in faithfulness; arrival and covenantal belonging are inseparable.
The prophet calls prisoners of hope to return to their stronghold, a compact return-to-safety image for threatened people.

basis: the ram's horn recalls the binding
note: The commentary identifies the hedy as an animal offering; this rabbinic teaching interprets the shofar as recalling the ram at Isaac's binding and its merit before God.
